orient: Narrator: Nelly Dean, continuing her story to Lockwood. It is late summer 1801. After months of letters, the dying Edgar has at last agreed that Cathy may meet her cousin Linton on the moors near the Grange, with Nelly as chaperone.

notes.g: Past its best; so it is late summer.

notes.m: 'Close' weather is stuffy and heavy, not 'near'.

notes.g: Patchy; mottled with light and dark.
A standing stone that marks the way across the moor.
notes.n: On open moorland, stone posts guided travellers in fog, snow or darkness. Lockwood noticed a line of such stones in Chapter III.

notes.g: The place where two roads or tracks cross.
A boy who looks after cattle or sheep.

notes.tr: Master Linton was just this side of the Heights, and he'd be much obliged if we would go on a little further.

notes.n: A northern and Scottish word, related to 'gangway'.

notes.t: the first injunction of his uncle
notes.n: An 'injunction' is a command or instruction. Edgar said they must stay on the moors nearest the Grange.

notes.g: The land belonging to Thrushcross Grange.

notes.t: our excursion shall lie towards home
notes.g: We'll ride in the direction of home.
About 400 metres; a few minutes' walk.
Let our horses feed on the grass.

notes.m: 'Ejaculation' meant any short, sudden exclamation. No sexual meaning.

notes.t: the congratulation on their long-postponed meeting
notes.g: Her happy greeting at finally meeting after so long.

notes.t: papa says I grow so fast
notes.g: My father says it's because I'm growing so fast.
notes.n: Growing too quickly was a common old excuse for a pale, weak teenager. Linton is repeating his father's words.

notes.g: Close to your idea of heaven.
notes.n: In Chapter XXIV Cathy told how they argued over the perfect summer day. Linton's was lying still on a bank of heath in bright sunshine; hers was rocking in a green tree in a breeze.

notes.g: The large grounds around Thrushcross Grange.
notes.n: A 'park' was the private enclosed land, lawns and woods around a country house.

notes.g: Keeping up any conversation at all.
A change that was hard to put a finger on.
Coaxed into affection by petting and soothing.
Gloomy, sullen concern with nothing but himself.
Someone who has become permanently sick.

notes.n: When Linton first came, Heathcliff ordered that he be looked after like a gentleman (Chapter XX). Nelly wonders whether that has turned into open cruelty.

notes.g: Small dark-blue wild berries that grow on the moors.
notes.n: Close relatives of blueberries; Americans might call them wild blueberries.

notes.g: What she found (a joking, grand phrase).

notes.n: 'Mighty' meaning 'very' was everyday British speech then, though now it sounds American.
A penance is a punishment someone accepts to make up for a sin.

notes.g: The dark, jutting spur of hill above us.
notes.n: 'Nab' is a northern word for a projecting knoll or point of a hill. Heathcliff used it in Chapter XXI.

notes.m: Just a friendly disagreement, not a serious quarrel.

notes.t: threw little light on his inquiries
notes.g: Told him little in answer to his questions.
